bull.t: Rapid Revenue Growth And Contracted Demand
bull.b: Exceptional revenue growth and a rapidly expanding backlog provide substantial forward visibility for the business. Large customer commitments can support continued infrastructure utilization, improve planning confidence, and reinforce CoreWeave’s position as a scaled provider of AI compute capacity.

bull.t: Strong Operating Leverage And Gross Economics
bull.b: High gross margins and sharply improved adjusted EBITDA indicate attractive economics as deployed capacity scales. If utilization and pricing remain supportive, this operating leverage can help absorb infrastructure costs and create a durable path toward stronger profitability over the next several quarters.

bull.t: Expanding AI Platform And Managed Inference
bull.b: Rapid adoption of managed inference broadens CoreWeave beyond infrastructure rental toward higher-value platform services. Growth in this offering can deepen customer relationships, diversify revenue within AI workloads, and increase the company’s relevance as customers move models from training into production.

bear.t: Very High Leverage Constrains Financial Flexibility
bear.b: The heavily debt-funded capital structure leaves CoreWeave more exposed to refinancing conditions, interest costs, and execution setbacks than a less leveraged infrastructure provider. High leverage can restrict capital allocation flexibility and increase the financial consequences of slower customer ramp or weaker utilization.

bear.t: Heavy Capital Spending Drives Negative Free Cash Flow
bear.b: The scale of required investment currently overwhelms operating cash generation, making continued expansion dependent on substantial financing and successful deployment. Large and accelerating CapEx also raises execution risk because returns depend on bringing new GPU capacity online and filling it with paying demand.

bear.t: Losses And Rising Interest Expense Impede Earnings Conversion
bear.b: CoreWeave’s strong revenue and adjusted EBITDA have not yet translated into GAAP profitability, as financing costs and ramp-related expenses remain substantial. Rising interest expense can consume an increasing share of operating gains, delaying retained-cash generation and limiting the durability of earnings improvement.
